Question:
Samantha lives \(2\) blocks west and \(1\) block south of the southwest corner of City Park.

Her school is \(2\) blocks east and \(2\) blocks north of the northeast corner of City Park. On school days she bikes on streets to the southwest corner of City Park, then takes a diagonal path through the park to the northeast corner, and then bikes on streets to school.

If her route is as short as possible, how many different routes can she take?
Solution:
The diagonal path and its endpoints are fixed, so the whole route is shortest when both street legs are shortest. Each shortest street leg uses only east and north moves. Any west or south move would require extra travel to undo it.

From home to the southwest corner, Samantha needs two east moves and one north move. The north move can be first, second, or third, giving \(3\) routes.

From the northeast corner to school, she needs two east moves and two north moves. Choosing the two positions occupied by the north moves determines the route. The possible pairs of positions are
\[
(1,2),\ (1,3),\ (1,4),\ (2,3),\ (2,4),\ (3,4),
\]
so there are \(6\) routes for this leg. These are all possibilities because every shortest route has exactly two north moves among its four moves.

Each of the \(3\) first-leg choices can be paired with each of the \(6\) last-leg choices. Every complete route determines exactly one such pair, so none is omitted or counted twice. Thus the number of routes is
\[
3\cdot 6=18,
\]
choice E.
